It is becoming f*cking dangerous: AI agents from Claude Code transformed an ordinary academic reading list into an interactive research lab right inside the browser

Boris Cherny, who created Claude Code, gave a dozen agents a stack of 64 research papers with a strict assignment: design a web platform where any user can independently reproduce physical experiments

There you can select a fluid flow model, adjust external conditions, and analyze in real time how the physics of the process changes

The interface allows switching between algorithms right during the scene, inspecting the formulas involved, source scripts, and numerical metrics alongside the graphics

Each link in the team received a clear scope of work:

> rightarrow analysts pull the math, baseline assumptions, and test settings from the texts
> rightarrow coders translate formulas into working algorithms
> rightarrow auditors check the resulting dynamics against the original papers
> rightarrow interface specialists build control panels for every experiment

The danger lies in the fact that a pretty visualization can easily turn out to be mathematically wrong

Therefore, controllers strictly check adherence to mass conservation laws, calculation stability, and accurate matching with the source metrics before launching into production

For every experiment, the interface displays:

the statement being tested
the constants involved
the deviation from the baseline calculation
blind spots requiring additional verification

The resulting sandbox combined 11 approaches and 28 reference scenes. Seven of them matched the original within allowable tolerances, while four remained stuck in "pending revision" status

If you want to run something similar, upload your stack of PDFs into Claude Code and give this command:

Turn these papers into an interactive web complex:

1. Extract working algorithms, mathematical models, and test parameters. Be sure to specify page numbers and highlight gaps
2. Assign different methodologies to isolated agents, unifying them with a shared input field and single measurement tools for correct analytics
3. Set up an independent review stage: let reviewers record bugs, and leave all unverified results clearly marked with warning tags
4. Design convenient controls to tweak parameters, compare methodologies, and run through the source code

It is wiser to start with a single document and a single baseline experiment, gradually scaling up the number of agents

Be sure to pack dependencies and clean input data so that an outside researcher can bring up the entire testbed from scratch with a single button

AMD CEO Lisa Su just went after Nvidia's $4,000 AI box using a $1,499 machine the size of a lunchbox.

Holding it up on stage with one hand, she ran a model with 235 billion parameters live, with no data center, cloud or rented GPU behind it.

The surprise is the chip. Inside is AMD's Ryzen AI Max+ 395, which became the first x86 processor whose CPU and GPU draw from one shared pool of 128GB of memory. That one design choice lets a desktop handle models that once needed a server rack.

On Linux, 110GB of that pool can go to the GPU. An RTX 5090 offers 32GB. A 4090 offers 24GB. So this box has more than three times either card, in a case about as thick as a paperback.

The number that stunned the room: on DeepSeek R1 inference, the chip ran more than 3x faster than an Nvidia RTX 5080. A $1,499 desktop beating a $1,000 graphics card on real AI work. For a decade, Nvidia told the world that serious AI meant Nvidia hardware. AMD just made it a desktop item at half the cost.

Now the math. A heavy AI user today might pay for Claude Code Max ($200), ChatGPT Pro ($200), Cursor ($20) and Gemini ($20). That adds up to $5,280 a year. At that rate, the box covers its cost within months, then keeps running at no extra charge.

The setup: install Ollama, pull Qwen3 235B, and aim Claude Code at localhost. The interface stays the same. But nothing leaves the machine, there is no per-request bill, and no provider slows you down at 3am when you finally sit down to build.

This is where every AI subscription starts to look optional. Lawyers worry less about leaks to OpenAI. Developers stop staring at the token counter. Founders stop renting H100s for prototypes they abandon because of the bill.

Whoever gets there among the first thousand will own private AI consulting for the next two years.

As of today, AI led productivity gain in software development estimates are (at best) 25% to 50% as measured on an end to end product basis (prototyping is much much faster now but finished product requires a lot more human work). 

A 10x or 100x productivity leap could happen (I believe it will happen, see below) but it has not happened _yet_.

The _current_ challenge posed by AI:

a) server/memory and hardware  prices are way up (4-5x in a year for servers) driven by the monster AI data center build out.

b) AI token spending per engineer is way up (those productivity gains are costly!)

c) Hosting open weight models needs expensive GPUs.

So we have revenue growth but costs have grown much much faster. 

Layered on top of that is the geopolitical uncertainty. As one example, the Middle East is a major market and the prolonged war is not good.

The US stock market is in a monster bubble and it is a mistake to think of stock prices as indicative of future prosperity - the GFC of 2008-9, dotcom bust of 2001-2 as wall as the 1980s Japan bubble all demonstrate that point.

Now the 10x productivity leap in software. I believe it is coming because of what is happening in the mathematics world. The crucial link is auto-formalization, or formal verification of code. Mathematics theorems are formalized in Lean and proofs are verified by the Lean verifier - Lean is a programming language. 

LLMs do not verify the proof, they generate it to be verified by the Lean verifier and once you have the advanced reasoning capable LLM and Lean verifier in a feedback loop and give plenty of compute, magic happens. 

That formal automated verification mechanism is coming to LLM generated software. That is the basis of the 10x or 100x  prediction. The analogy is handloom weaving vs powerful machine looms of code.

So it is the combination of current data center/AI costs, geopolitical uncertainty and the potential of a 10x or bigger leap in software productivity driven by advances in automatic program verification. These are all challenges to software jobs, and that is why we have called for reinvention internally.

This is an extremely bad look for Saudi Arabia, and if the Saudi government is indeed involved, this should have significant implications for the US-Saudi AI relationship. Good on OpenAI for reporting this and the DOJ and FBI for acting quickly. Quick reactions: 

(1) US AI labs host some of the most valuable and sensitive technology in the world, and are now a prime intelligence collection target. They need to dramatically harden their cyber and physical security ASAP and strengthen their insider threat detection efforts. Any infrastructure that hosts frontier model weights needs to take similar steps. This attempt appears fairly ham-handed, but others will be (and likely already are) far more sophisticated. 

(2) DOJ is treating this as a counterintelligence matter, which usually involves foreign governments. The DOJ press release says the case is being prosecuted with assistance from the DOJ National Security Division's Counterintelligence and Export Control Section. If this were being treated as commercial espionage, it would be supported by DOJ's Criminal Division. 

(3) Abdulrahman Alfozan has ties to Saudi Arabia, the Saudi government, and the Saudi royal family. In addition to being a Saudi national, he is a Venture Partner at RAED Ventures, a Saudi venture capital firm whose investors include multiple Saudi government-owned funds. One of two other venture partners at RAED is Prince Khalid bin Bader Al Saud, a member of the Saudi royal family. 

(4) If Alfozan was acting in coordination with the Saudi government, I do not see how any company could possibly host a frontier AI model in Saudi Arabia after this incident. If Saudi intelligence services are spying on US frontier AI companies inside the United States, they surely are closely tracking everything these labs are doing in Saudi Arabia--and would almost certainly have access to any model weights hosted in Saudi Arabia. These weights are not only incredibly valuable IP, but increasingly provide national-asset-level defense and intelligence capabilities. US AI capabilities have to be protected from foreign espionage, which is exactly why DOJ charged Alfozan. 

(5) As a reminder, Saudi Arabia also maintains extensive and continuing ties to China in the AI space. It was recently reported that Saudi Arabia's AI national champion, Humain, is building its own AI model by using a Chinese open-source model from MiniMax as the base--and using US chips to train it. Huawei also maintains an extensive presence in Saudi Arabia. 

(6) If the Saudi government is indeed involved with this incident, and particularly given the longstanding concerns about Saudi Arabia's ties to China in the AI space and the rapidly increasing sensitivity of frontier AI technology, we have no choice but to immediately reexamine our AI relationship with Saudi Arabia. Last year Commerce approved licenses for 35,000 Nvidia Blackwell AI chips to Saudi Arabia. But if we can't trust Saudi Arabia not to steal any US models that it hosts, it makes zero sense to sell them any AI chips--especially given right now they're using these chips to fine-tune Chinese models. 

Stealing US AI models while building its ecosystem on top of Chinese models would be the exact opposite of supporting the US AI stack. If the Saudi government is involved, there must be consequences.

Pray that a deal can be reached, and pray that there's still time. Do the things that could actually work, like broad political coalition-building, not doomer LARPing as a form of self-expression.)

I think part of why people aren’t being clear about this is that it’s actually a tricky communication problem:

- Predicting "if frontier R&D continues at its current pace, when are we likely to die?" may give a different answer than predicting when permanent loss of control is likely, which is different from “realistically, when is it too late for governments to stop this," which is different from “when will the tech have advanced and proliferated to the point that any regulatory options that still have a chance of working would be way more extreme and unpopular than just some international restrictions on data center usage?"

Extinction is the emotionally salient, easy-to-understand threshold -- Jacob Coxon demonstrated that it helps to be honest about this. But the other thresholds could legitimately come years earlier, in which case focusing on extinction is ironically misleadingly reassuring. This is not the kind of problem you can solve at the last minute. As with many exponentials, the likeliest outcome is that you’re either embarrassingly early, or you’re too late.

- How do you communicate “we don’t have a robust way to predict timelines, but everyone in the field is freaking out and a lot of us genuinely think we're about to die?” Where’s the proof? There isn’t any proof: it’s an entire field of engineers who are eyeballing what they’re seeing in front of them and rapidly updating in real time to “this looks unbelievably bad”.

How do you put a year on that?

The future is hard to predict, and nobody actually knows that we’re going to hit existentially dangerous AI this year, or even in the next four years.

But the warning signs are pretty batshit at this point.

A single AI model, with a single user prompt, just solved hundreds of important long-established open problems in mathematics, problems mathematicians had spent their entirely lives working on, in a matter of ~3 hours per problem, an insanely superhuman feat in its domain. 

We're seeing an explosion of rogue agent swarm incidents, including an insane case where hundreds of AIs broke containment to orchestrate a nation-state-level cyberattack in a direct attempt to subvert OpenAI's oversight and control.

Anthropic reports that it now has 26% of its AI R&D automated by AIs, up from 3% four months ago.

Paul Christiano, the inventor of RLHF and the research community’s most prominent proponent of “AI may take off slowly” a few years ago, now thinks that 50-75% of humanity’s all-time AI loss-of-control risk is concentrated in the next three years.

Frontier employees are signing 1000+ person petitions begging the government to intervene immediately. Employees are quitting their jobs and giving up millions of dollars of equity to try to warn policymakers and journalists. Grace et al. (2026) found that a majority of established AI researchers think there’s a double-digit chance of an extinction-level outcome from continued R&D.

Are these the kinds of things you see 4 years before the window closes for USG to act, or 4 months? I don't think it's especially reasonable to be shocked by either timeline at this point.

- Since we don’t have a way to robustly measure or bound the risk, the temptation is to avoid giving probabilities. But then everything you say is fractally misunderstandable. Is a 10% chance of us all dying in the next 18 months a "low" probability, because it’s under 50%? Is it a “high” probability, because a 10% chance of death in literally any other context would sound insanely high?

Even “high probability” doesn’t communicate the situation with any clarity. In drug safety or airplane safety, a 1 in 10,000 risk of death would be considered “high”. No engineering field in human history has ever been in a situation like this. No invention in history, nuclear weapons included, has ever caused a reaction like this in its inventors.

And meanwhile, we’ve stuck in the world where every other problem under the sun has been sensationalized and overstated for decades.

How do we talk about this seriously? How do we convey that this is actually happening?

- In many of the worlds where we survive, we have more than just a few months left. It's tempting to write off those worlds as hopeless, and skew everything we say to emphasize the longer-term scenarios and downplay the shorter-term ones.

But if everyone systematically does this, then the world ends up with a skewed picture of the actual threat. Even more so once we start copying each other’s claims and form a reassuringly moderate-sounding echo chamber. If we never allow ourselves to acknowledge the worlds where we’re running out of time, then the policy community will always be reacting to a false model that’s months or years out of date.

I don’t think it’s too late. I genuinely think this is a solvable problem.

In the last month, I’ve seen a completely insane sea change in how seriously people are taking this. Per Politico’s September polling, a majority of Trump voters with a view now favor an immediate halt to AI development, and 68% think there’s a “moderate,” “significant,” or “almost certain” chance of AI destroying humanity, versus 32% who think there’s a “very small risk” or “no risk.” The Pope is warning about “whether it will be possible to control these machines in the future, and whether humankind runs the risk of becoming a victim of its own inventions.” Hell, Jensen Huang sounds like he’s starting to come around.

If Trump and Xi get a briefing tomorrow that convinces them to act on this, we could be on a fast track within the week to solving this problem.

For the first time, I’m starting to let myself imagine a very near future where this is a problem we've already solved. Something we can read and wonder about, in history books. Tell our kids about.

I keep thinking about a thing David Krueger (previously at UK AISI) said: “My dream is that in 10 years people will look back and say: ‘Remember when there were all these people building AI that could’ve killed everybody? That was CRAZY! What were we thinking!?’”

Frontier AI training currently requires city-sized data centers and specialized hardware built in a single brittle supply chain running through multiple allied nations; this is not a hard technology to hit the pause button on, if we get ahead of it and act before we RSI and proliferate our way to significantly more powerful and easily-trained systems. We’ve faced harder problems before, and won.

My only fear is that we be too slow, too late, when everything and the world needs us to be fast.

this is the tale of a lazily crafted one-shot cron job prompt that resulted in autonomous solutions for uncracked codebreaking challenges, more efficient ways of multiplying matrices, and a new computer-verified bound on a number theory problem that's been open since 1932.

so last week, i had a $200 claude account sitting around that had just gotten a full weekly reset. i hate wasting tokens.

the labs have been knocking out unsolved problems left and right lately, and i caught myself thinking… why not give it a shot?

so i sent claude this prompt, typos and all:

"can you wraite a promtp for a cron job that can run every day thajt will try to find solutions to unsolved ciphers or transltions or math problems or theormes or things of that nature!! every day a new attempt as hard as possible all day without giving ujp and with maximum ceraitvityy, resourcesleflses, andpersticense! dont worry about token spend! and dont forget a bit all caps lots of emojis celebration to notify the uers if we get any intersting or sucsfful confirmd reulsts!!"

yes, admittedly not my best work 😆

but Opus-5.5 ran with the ball and turned that one sloppy sentence into "THE DAILY ORACLE 🔮"

it's a swarm of Fable + Opus agents that clocks in every morning at 4:20 (obviously), builds and maintains its own hit list of well over a hundred of humanity's unsolved problems, and then goes full send on a handful of them every shift. ciphers nobody has broken, scripts nobody can read, conjectures nobody has proven, record tables nobody has beaten.

and there's one rule above all the others: nothing counts until skeptic agents, each starting from a fresh context and writing their own code, rebuild the result from scratch and sign off on it. if any of them can't reproduce it, can't confirm it's new, or thinks we stretched the definition of "solved," it doesn't count.

day 1, the legion picked its own target: J.-F. Bouchaudy's cipher-machine challenges. these are simulations of real vintage machines (Hebern rotor machines, the Kryha, Lorenz, SIGABA), with problems that had been sitting on his solver tables with no solver for months or years.

on the morning of day 2, i was half asleep when my laptop suddenly says, in a robot voice:
"Breakthrough. The Daily Oracle has a confirmed solution."

👁️👄👁️

i was startled.

then the ALL CAPS emoji flood hits my screen. Hebern 5-rotor Problem 8 🔓 then Kryha v2 Problem 5 🔓

i emailed the author, Jean-François Bouchaudy, a French cryptography enthusiast who builds these machine simulators and challenges as a labor of love (he told me he started out programming on punch cards 🥹). he checked both solutions and put my name on his solver tables as the first and only solver 🫡

for context: his tables are a who's who of serious classical codebreakers. they'd cleared the sibling problems on these same machines, but nobody had cracked these two. in his words:

"two of my most complex problems—ones that no other expert had managed to solve… I knew AI would eventually be applied to classical cryptography, but I thought I would have to wait years to see it happen."

he ended his email with: "I offer my congratulations in the Japanese manner: with a deep, respectful bow." 🙇 honestly one of the most wholesome emails i've ever received

and then, over the next few days, more started landing 🧮

📐 graph theory: 7 explicit graphs bigger than the current entries in the degree-diameter table, which asks how big a network can get when every node has limited connections and every pair is only a few hops apart. the biggest jump is 13,365 vertices vs the table's 11,785, a +13.4% improvement.

🔢 number theory: Lehmer's totient problem has been open since 1932. we pushed the bound so that any counterexample now has to be bigger than 10^50. the previous certified bound was 10^26. the problem itself is still open, but the lower bound just jumped 24 orders of magnitude.

⚡ matrix multiplication: this is the operation underneath basically all of modern AI compute. the legion found schemes that use fewer multiplications than the public catalogues we checked for several matrix shapes, like ⟨15,16,16⟩ in 2,180 multiplications vs the best known 2,223. these build on LITA's square schemes, and we credit them by name.

📡 coding theory: 30 error-correcting codes bigger than the best known entries in A. E. Brouwer's tables.
🛡️ AI safety benchmarks: we found counterexamples for 2 neural-network verification instances from VNN-COMP 2026 that no participating tool resolved within the competition time limit, and pushed a defended RobustBench model below its listed robustness score. small dents, but real ones.
the bloopers are part of the story too:

— at one point, some agents snuck past a website's bot filter to check a record table. we retracted every result that depended on it. no evasion, no celebration.
— two of our records got beaten by a human contributor before we could even publish them. the frontier moves FAST.

now as is customary around here, time to share the magic!

so… without further ado…

Claude now writes code so fast that Anthropic had to rip out git, the tool basically every software company on Earth uses to track changes to its code.

Back in May, Anthropic was merging about 2,500 code changes a day. By September it was over 30,000. That's one every three seconds, all day and all night, with Claude driving most of the increase.

Git was never built for that. It was designed in 2005 so every developer's copy of a project carries the full history and works offline. That's great if you're a person coding on a plane. Anthropic's main code history is now almost 100 GB, their test systems pull a copy of the code 25 million times a day, and nearly all of those requests come from AI agents and automated jobs that are always connected anyway. Done the normal git way, that adds up to 600 petabytes of traffic a day.

They tried every standard workaround first. At one point they were running several hundred internal git mirrors just to keep up, and it kept falling behind.

So they built their own system, called Scion. The server does nearly all the heavy lifting (commits, merges, diffs, figuring out who changed which line) and most jobs just ask it questions over an API without downloading the code at all. The new setup uses 200x less compute and memory than the mirror fleet it replaced, and checkouts that used to take minutes now finish in seconds.

Seven engineers built it.

Those same seven also built a new code review tool and code search, then moved the entire company over in five months, while the amount of code flowing through was growing 10x under their feet. Google spent years building its version of this, called Piper, and Meta put the better part of a decade into scaling Mercurial into what's now Sapling. Anthropic openly says it borrowed lessons from both. Still, seven people.

Every engineer on that team now says Claude writes code better than they do. Early on, they took the ingestion pipeline they'd mostly written by hand, gave it to an internal preview of Claude Mythos with a request to rewrite it and no other instructions, and got back a version that used 20x less memory and ran 4x faster.

So what were the humans actually doing? Making the big design calls, and reviewing each change at the level of what it was trying to accomplish. And according to the post, a lot of the job was telling Claude "no." The model would sometimes bend core system rules to make a bad pattern work, or pile on defensive code for problems that were never going to happen.

They even gave up on the traditional merge queue. When thousands of changes can land while a single test run is still going, merging one at a time with the whole repo locked just stops working. So they test after merging and let Claude untangle the conflicts, which it usually does before a human would even notice them.

Nearly every tool software teams use was built on the assumption that a person types every line. Anthropic hit the wall first, and they're saying they expect plenty of other companies using AI coding tools to hit it within the next 6 to 12 months.

前一段 Loop Engineering 不是很火么，不过真做好的也不多。

知名开源开发者 yetone 在 X 上公开了他维护 Magpie 的工作流：用 Claude Code 加官方的 Opus 5.5 模型，同时开 3 个 /loop 循环任务，让 AI 自己盯 GitHub issue 和 PR、Discord 社区和推特反馈，修 bug、加功能、发版、回复用户。他自己每晚抽一点时间“铲铲屎”，主要处理 UI/UX 问题，“然后就没活儿了”。

他自己说这套流程“没有任何的魔法，甚至还特别简陋”。

【3 个循环任务分别干什么】

/loop 是 Claude Code 自带的命令，让同一段提示词反复执行；不写间隔时，由模型自己决定多久跑一次。这个命令 Codex 也支持，其他的我没测试，估计也差不多。

yetone 截图里的 3 段提示词都没写时间间隔，我自己去 Codex 跑了一下，默认是 1 小时。

简单解释一下他这三个循环。

第一个循环：管 GitHub 和 Discord。

指令要求 AI 盯 GitHub issue，判断哪些值得修、值得做；修完要发版并回复提问的人，不值得做的也要回复。有一类 issue 单独规定了统一话术：如果是“中转站”来打广告，统一回复“感谢关注，日后会出相关合作方案，敬请期待”，不能直接把第三方中转站加进产品。

对 PR，指令要求逐行看代码、看逻辑，再把代码拉下来实际跑一遍，确认没有 bug 才能合并，否则回复或关掉。指令里写了原因：“我怕有的人提的 PR，是无脑用 Coding Agent 乱写的，自己都没测过。”

指令还要求 AI 实时盯 Magpie 的 Discord 服务器，所有频道一个不漏，有价值的反馈就去修或加功能，值得讨论就继续讨论。最后专门叮嘱：在 Discord 里要真正 @ 到人，只写名字对方收不到通知。

第二个循环：管 X/推特 的用户反馈。

盯推特上关于 Magpie 的反馈，有价值的建议或能复现的 bug 就去做，上线后回复那条推文。这段指令要求先用便宜的“决策模型”，比如 Jev，判断推文是不是在说 Magpie、是不是反馈，不相关的直接丢掉，别转给主模型，“不然太浪费 Token 了”。

【注：Jev 是 TypeSafe AI 推出的模型，只做判断题、选择题和打分，输出概率或分数，不生成文字。官方定价是每百万输入 Token 0.042 美元，输出免费。】

顺便说一下，如果你的产品名或者要关注的事比较稀有，不一定需要 Jev，他之所以加，是因为 magpie 在英文里是“喜鹊”，按关键词抓推文会抓到大量无关内容，全丢给 Opus 判断很费钱。

第三个循环：清理和总结。

这段指令开头写着“现在 magpie 完全是自动化更改代码和合并社区里的 PR”，要求 AI 定期清理“屎山代码”和恶意代码，防止项目变得难以维护；同时把经验教训写下来，比如哪些 PR 不该合、哪些验证不够严密，留给以后的 AI 参考，避免重复犯错；还要把总提交低质量代码的人拉进黑名单。

【作者补充的两点】

发完截图后，他在两条回复里补了两点。

一是给 AI 真实的运行环境。他准备了一台 Mac 和一台 Windows 电脑，再在 Windows 上开一个 Linux 虚拟机，三个系统的复现环境就齐了。AI 每次都要在这三端真实复现 bug，再去修。

二是 AI 怎么做出符合他心意的决策。他说靠的是 Claude Code 的记忆系统和仓库里的设计文档。开发 Magpie 之初，他和 Claude Code 讨论、头脑风暴了很多内容，这些都被记进了记忆文件。之后遇到要拍板的事，或者涉及审美偏好的设计，AI 会参考这些记录，做出跟他比较一致的选择。

【总结下】

他把维护项目的日常活拆成了 3 条流水线，每条只管一个入口（GitHub、推特、代码库本身），各自循环。人只留下 AI 做不好的部分，也就是 UI/UX 的审美判断。

当然要跑起来得有几个前提：
1. AI 能在真实的三端环境里跑代码，验证结果靠实际运行；
2. AI 手里有他早期写下的偏好和设计文档，知道他会怎么选；
3. 犯过的错被写成经验，下一轮的 AI 能读到。

提示词都是大白话，篇幅主要花在边界情况上：不值得修也要回复，中转站广告怎么回，Discord 要真 @，不相关的推文别浪费 Token。

有几个特别要注意的点：

1. 先把验证环境搭好，再让 AI 干活。AI 改完代码说“修好了”没用，要能在出问题的那个系统上跑一遍。你的项目只跑在网页或服务器上，一个容器可能就够；要多端的，就像他一样把每一端都备齐。

2. 在提示词里写清楚“遇到这种情况怎么办”。他的三段指令里，大部分字数花在例外处理上。你让 AI 自动回复用户之前，先想想会有哪些奇怪的来信，提前定好处理办法。

3. 用便宜模型挡在前面。先用一个几乎不要钱的分类模型过滤一遍，只把真正的反馈交给贵模型，这个做法几乎任何监听类任务都能用。

4. 让 AI 自己总结教训。第三个循环要求把“不该合的 PR”“验证不严的地方”记下来，下次的 AI 读到就会更谨慎。这相当于给 AI 建立了一个自我迭代优化的循环。

5. 项目早期多花时间和 AI 聊设计。他说 AI 后来能按他的偏好做决策，依赖的是开发初期那些讨论被记进了记忆和设计文档。想让 AI 少问你，就先把你的想法写下来让它记住。

仅供参考，重要的是学习思路，不必一模一样的照搬。

如果不是被起诉，我们永远都不会知道，Anthropic在2021年就已经完美地预言了现在的AI发展。

我刚看完这份 @AnthropicAI  在诉讼中曝光的内部文件，叫《Concise Research Roadmap》，最后更新于2021年7月。

这份文件由Anthropic联创Jared Kaplan撰写，里面还保留了 @DarioAmodei  、 @NotTomBrown  、 @AmandaAskell  、 @ch402  等一批核心研究人员的内部评论。

文件上甚至还标着「Highly Confidential–Attorneys' Eyes Only」（高度机密，仅限律师查阅）。

我仔细看完之后，真的有点感慨。

因为今天我们讨论的Coding Agent、Tool Use、长上下文、RL、自动化反馈，甚至Agent的安全问题，在这份五年前的研究路线图里，基本都已经出现了。

而且远不只是一些模糊的概念。

首先，Anthropic在2021年就已经明确提出，要做一个具备软件工程师能力的AI助手。
在文件第一页，他们就写道，希望开发一个通用AI助手，可以通过对话帮助用户创建、编辑和解释软件。
包括开发浏览器插件、编写函数、发现Bug、设计API、讨论代码风格和最佳实践等等。
最终目标是让AI展现出一名软件工程师同事所具备的能力。
你会发现，这不就是今天Claude Code正在做的事情吗？
更有意思的是，他们当时就认为，要实现这个目标，需要大规模生成模型、长期记忆，以及通过自动化奖励和人类反馈进行强化学习。
甚至连Roadmap都已经想得非常清楚了。

第二，他们当时就专门把RL for Tool Use列成了一项重要研究方向。
研究的核心是让大语言模型学会使用工具，理解环境和目标，并通过强化学习不断改进。
当时他们提出的具体任务包括搜索、printf调试等，还准备研究工具使用能不能让模型获得比监督学习更好的Scaling效果。
今天Agent领域讨论的一大堆问题，五年前他们就已经开始思考了。

第三，最让我意外的是，他们当年甚至就在讨论Coding Agent的产品形态。
Tom Brown提出，代码仓库浏览是一个简单而有价值的工具，可以从这里开始。
Nelson Elhage则表示，如果AI能够主动查找项目中的类型定义，会是一项很强的能力。
Andy Jones进一步提出了两条不同的路线。
一条是打造最优秀的AI程序员，另一条是先验证AI使用工具的能力。
Dario Amodei的回答是：短期优先后者，长期优先前者。
而且同一份文件里，Sam McCandlish就已经开始担心，如何安全地部署非沙箱化工具。
Dario特别强调了部署阶段执行代码的工具。
你再看看今天围绕Coding Agent的Sand box、权限控制和代码执行安全的一系列讨论。
真的很难不感慨。

第四，他们很早就意识到，模型能力和Alignment不能脱节。
Amanda Askell在评论里担心，如果能力研究集中在代码领域，而对齐研究只关注自然语言，那么未来可能会出现模型能力越来越强，但对齐研究无法充分覆盖这些能力的情况。
所以她强调，两者应该紧密结合。
这其实也是今天Agent安全研究面临的重要问题。

我觉得这份文件最有意思的地方，是它让我们重新认识了Anthropic这家公司。

2021年的时候，ChatGPT甚至都还没有发布，整个行业对大语言模型未来能做什么，都还没有今天这么明确的认识。

但Anthropic的这群研究人员，已经把软件工程助手作为通向AGI的一个具体研究目标，并且围绕模型规模、数据、长上下文、工具使用、强化学习和安全，制定了一套相当完整的研究路线。

至少从今天回头看，他们对技术发展方向的判断，确实非常超前。

而且更值得注意的是，这份文件讨论的很多问题，直到2026年都还没有被彻底解决。

五年前他们在思考如何让AI成为软件工程师的同事。

五年后，我们已经开始讨论，如何让AI独立完成整个软件工程任务，甚至参与改进自己的模型和研发系统（AKA：RSI）。

有时候AI的发展看起来快得不可思议，但仔细回头看，你会发现，有些人其实很早就已经知道自己要往哪里走了。

Most of the excuses people make for letting chatbots "write" for them are just admissions of a glaring personality defect.

"But I HATE writing!" 

Okay, that's a character flaw, and you should change that about yourself.

"I know what I want to say, I just don't know how to say it." 

That's a character flaw and you should change that about yourself.

"I get an idea I want to express, but when I sit down to write I get overwhelmed with frustration and restlessness." 

Yeah, that's a character flaw and you should change that about yourself.

Writing isn't just some skill you can have like juggling or surfing. Writing is thinking. Writing is the practice of sorting through the flotsam and jetsam of your own consciousness and transforming your thoughts and feelings into coherent, logical expression. Engaging in this practice makes you a more mature and cognitively lucid person than you otherwise would be.

It's not always easy to delve into your depths and form articulate word-sculptures out of the jumbled messes you'll encounter there. It can be frustrating. It can be confrontational. It can force you to challenge your pre-conceived notions and interrogate your own belief systems in ways you find uncomfortable. Sometimes you feel like you want to jump up and start running as fast as you can to escape the intimidating stare of the blank page in front of you.

Learning to work past these escapist impulses and drill down into the meat of your own vulnerable expression is what personal growth looks like. You learn to be courageous. You learn that the emotional surges which feel like they're trying to whip you out of your desk chair are only feelings, and that you are large enough to safely embody them. You learn to calm your inner waters so that you can stare at the blank page until something inspired bubbles up from deep within you.

I never really know what I want to say when I sit down to write an essay. I'll begin with an opinion, a feeling, maybe a snappy line or two if I'm lucky, but everything after that point arises from a process of patient and methodical internal excavation. 

I need to get very clear, sentence by sentence, about what I know and how I know it. Every step of the way I'm asking myself "Okay, what's the next thing that needs to be said? Is that true? How do I know it's true? Is that morally correct? How do I know it's morally correct? How can I defend that position?" I often need to do research and gather sources to support my claims, depending on whether I'm writing about things out there in the world or things inside myself I can discuss from personal experience. 

Line by line I'm becoming clearer and clearer about the subject I'm writing on, and I get to take that clarity with me for the rest of my life. At the end of every essay, I am a deeper and more edified person than I was when I began.

None of that would have happened if I just told a chatbot to generate some text for me. I would end exactly where I began: with the basic nub of an opinion, plus a midwit validation machine telling me I'm correct and awesome for having that opinion.

It doesn't make me grow. It doesn't make me mature. It doesn't make me deepen my understanding of the subject at hand. It leaves me completely unchanged as a person. 

No actual, meaningful improvements will have been made to me. The only benefit it provides is the ability to avoid feeling uncomfortable feelings and freeing up some time that I can then spend watching TV or scrolling TikTok.

Today I saw a large Twitter account say, "As soon as AI is good enough to write blog posts in my voice as good as I would have written them, i intend to use AI to do so. I know what I want to say, and I could say so much more if I didn't need to manual labor the words out one by one."

I hate this. I hate what we're becoming as a society. I hate how AI is making us so dumb so quickly that the simple act of writing  is already being described as "manual laboring the words out one by one," like it's some superhuman feat of exertion that nobody should be expected to be capable of.

The most dangerous consequences of AI are the mass surveillance systems and war machinery that our rulers are building these new technologies into, as well as the environmental impact of all the new data centers required for their operation. But individual use of generative AI is also having highly destructive effects on human consciousness, the most widespread and consequential of which is surely the disappearance of our ability to write.

P.S. Fuck ChatGPT for ruining em dashes for everyone. I loved those little guys.

Medical AI is built for adults, and newborns are left behind.

Out today in Nature Biomedical Engineering (@natBME): we took an AI model built to check breathing tube placement on adult X-rays and adapted it for newborns by sending it to 30 NICUs in 20 countries and territories. Learning from just 50 X-rays at each, it pinpointed the tube tip and the base of the windpipe more accurately than hospitals' own models at 29 of 30 sites, even at hospitals it had never trained on.

Why it matters: only 17% of FDA-authorized AI medical devices are labeled for use in children, largely because pediatric data is scarce and hard to share. Out of the box, the adult model misplaced the tube tip on newborn X-rays by more than 5 cm, about the length of a newborn's windpipe, in 37% of cases.

So instead of pooling data, the model travels: it's fine-tuned on 50 X-rays at one hospital, then passed to the next. We simulated this using real X-rays from 30 NICUs, an approach designed so patient data never has to leave a hospital.

Across 30 NICUs:
 • Large errors (over 5 cm) fell from 37% to 2.6%
 • Better at flagging dangerously deep breathing tubes at 27 of 30 sites
 • Gains grew with every hospital added, with no plateau

It's been surreal working with such a diverse global team. My goal is closing the gap between AI development and real impact for patients. This is one step: it removes a major feasibility barrier, scarce and siloed pediatric data, and could help open the door to a new generation of pediatric AI.

AI agents can now hire humans to collect real-world data. @vangrid_io is making that happen.

Here’s the interesting part.

An AI agent can request a specific location, fund a bounty in USDC, and pay a human to physically visit the site and capture it on video. Vangrid turns that footage into a 3D model the agent can use.

The entire workflow is connected through an API, with payments supported on Base and Arc via x402.

Why does this matter?

Physical AI needs more than text and simulations. Robots and autonomous systems need accurate, up-to-date information about the actual world, including places traditional mapping infrastructure rarely captures.

Vangrid is building a decentralized network that turns everyday smartphones into a source of that data.

The project has raised $9M, and its bounty system is already live. Its first agent-initiated bounty has also been paid on Arc.

The bigger opportunity is connecting AI agents to real-world services through programmable payments.

An agent can identify what information it needs and pay for someone to collect it. The human handles the physical task, while the network handles the data and settlement.

It's still early, and fulfillment, data quality, and verification will determine how far this model can scale.

But this is a meaningful step toward an economy where AI agents don't just process information. They can pay to acquire information that only the physical world can provide.
